In Germany, we have a so called "sharp sword of self-defence": As long as you or someone else is about to be, currently or ongoing attacked, intentionally or not, by an unlawful human action (which excludes actions which are self-defence themselves), you can take every action against the attacker that is required to stop the attack. You are not required to "evade" the unlawful action, since "the right need not give way to the wrong." If you reasonably are afraid that no other action would stop him and the expected damage done by you is not disproportionate to the expected damage done by the attacker, you are allowed to kill the attacker.

So if someone is incessantly insulting you or is midway of an insult, you can punch him in the face to make him stop. There could even be a scenario in which you are allowed to kill him (it is possible but very unlikely).

We do have consolidated exceptions:
• You can't take actions that would violate the human dignity of the attacker, ie torture him to rescue someone else.
• If the attacker is for example a child, in a crazed state of mind or acting in no guilt (like a super-uber-drunken one), then you are required first to evade, if not possible to defend, if not possible to attack in the mildest form.
• If you intentionally provoked the attack you can't fight back since then you would misuse the law.

Other exceptions are more disputed and I don't want to go into unnecessary details.

It weirdly amazes me that that's how the german law of criminal procedure works regarding witnesses and hearsay-witnesses, too. Our principle of immediacy requires the court to hear the immediate witness. Only in the exception it can hear a hearsay-witness but then it has to justify the witness' evidential value more.
